title: India–Japan

cards.b:
India–Japan is often called the least problematic great-power relationship India has. There are no border disputes, no history of war between them, and a shared worry about China's rise.

Japan matters for India in four ways: capital (Official Development Assistance and investment), technology (Shinkansen, automobiles, electronics), security (Quad, Malabar) and ideas (the Indo-Pacific concept).

The weak point is trade. Bilateral trade is only about $23 billion, small for two of Asia's major economies. Exam questions often ask why the strategic and economic sides do not match.

cards.h: From sympathy to 'Special Strategic and Global Partnership'
cards.b:
Goodwill dates from Justice Radhabinod Pal, the Indian judge at the Tokyo Tribunal who dissented, and from India's decision not to claim war reparations. India signed a separate peace treaty in 1952.

Japan was the first country to give India a yen loan (1958). After the 1991 crisis it was a lender and investor. After 1998 Japan sanctioned India over its nuclear tests, but ties recovered by 2000. Shinzo Abe then made India a priority.

In August 2007 Abe addressed India's Parliament with a speech titled 'Confluence of the Two Seas', borrowing a phrase from the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh. He argued the Pacific and Indian Oceans were joining into a 'broader Asia'.

This idea fed the first Quad meeting (2007) and later Japan's 'Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)' strategy, announced at TICAD VI in Nairobi in 2016. India's own Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI) followed in 2019.

Abe's visit as Republic Day chief guest (2014) and his close friendship with Modi gave the partnership personal momentum. Abe was assassinated in July 2022. Modi declared a day of national mourning.

• 2008: Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation.
  • 2+2 dialogue (foreign and defence ministers) since 2019.
  • ACSA (2020): Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement for logistics.
  • Exercises: JIMEX (navy), Dharma Guardian (army), Shinyuu Maitri (air), and the Malabar exercise with the US and Australia (Japan a permanent member from 2015).
  • Quad: a core member of the grouping.
  • Technology: talks on defence equipment and technology; Japan's relaxation of its arms-export rules in 2014 made such cooperation possible.

The 16th annual summit in New Delhi (1–3 July 2026, with PM Sanae Takaichi) reportedly signed 16 deals, including AI, defence and maritime security. Japan is an Indo-Pacific security partner, though it has no alliance with India.

The Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) came into force in 2011. Japan is a top-five investor with cumulative FDI over $40 billion.

  • Mumbai–Ahmedabad High Speed Rail (MAHSR): a 508 km Shinkansen-based line, funded largely by a low-interest JICA yen loan. Work is behind schedule; the first section is targeted for the late 2020s.
  • Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor and the Delhi Metro, a showpiece of Japanese aid.
  • Act East Forum: Japanese roads and power in India's Northeast.
  • Maruti Suzuki: the 1983 joint venture made Japan a household name in India.

Investment goals rose over time: ¥3.5 trillion (2014–19), ¥5 trillion (2022–27) and a new target of ¥10 trillion over ten years set in 2025 and reaffirmed in July 2026.

Japan, the only country attacked with nuclear weapons, signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement with India on 11 November 2016. It entered into force on 20 July 2017.

It was historic because India is outside the NPT. The deal came with a Japanese statement that cooperation would stop if India conducted a nuclear test.

It matters in practice because Japanese firms supply key heavy components for reactors that other countries build. Heavy forgings for reactors worldwide come from Japanese suppliers, so the deal helped US and French reactor projects planned in India.

Japan and India also link in third countries. The Asia-Africa Growth Corridor (AAGC), announced in 2017, aims at quality infrastructure in Africa as an alternative to Belt and Road. They have discussed joint projects in third countries such as Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

Both support supply-chain resilience. In 2021 India, Japan and Australia launched the Supply Chain Resilience Initiative (SCRI). The Quad's critical minerals work followed.

India, Japan, Germany and Brazil form the G4, pressing for UN Security Council reform.

Japan's constitution (Article 9) limits its use of force, so it cannot act as a full military ally. Japanese firms complain of Indian red tape, land acquisition and tax disputes. India is not part of RCEP, which includes Japan and China.

Scholars like Purnendra Jain and Rajaram Panda describe the relationship as a 'values-plus-interest' partnership. Realists see it as balancing against China.

• Japan is a model for capital and quality infrastructure, without political strings.
  • It supports India's bid for a permanent UNSC seat and NSG membership.
  • Japan wants a stable India as a balancer in Asia as China and the US both turn more demanding.
  • The Northeast and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands receive Japanese projects of strategic value.

In 2025–26 the US tariff shock pushed India and Japan closer on supply chains, semiconductors and rare earths. Japan's new government under Sanae Takaichi (since October 2025) continued the partnership with a stronger focus on economic security and defence technology.

"Discuss the strategic dimensions of the India-Japan partnership." (typical)
"India-Japan relations are strong strategically but weak economically. Examine." (typical)
"What is the significance of Japan's role in the Indo-Pacific for India?" (typical)

Structure: (1) history: 1952, 1958, 2000, 2006, 2014; (2) Abe's 2007 speech and the Indo-Pacific; (3) security: 2+2, ACSA, Malabar, Quad; (4) economy: CEPA, MAHSR, ¥10 trillion target; (5) civil nuclear deal (2016); (6) limits and way forward.
